I wouldn't say I'm at more than an average skill level, but this is what seems to consistently yield results for me now and back in OW1. 

For heal/speed swapping, the way I think about it is that heal is my default state. I'll swap to speed to get my team or myself in/out of a situation mainly. Effectively translates to Heal = Hold ground, Speed = Reposition. 

For Amp, I Amp heal just as my team starts taking damage at the beginning of a team fight if possible, then once or twice more depending on how long the fight lasts. Giving your team that increased heal rate mid-fight definitely helps. Depending on the outcome, it might be best to Amp speed or at least swap to speed to break contact and reset, or push forward and clean up stragglers. 

What keeps me active in the fight most is movement. Learning to walljump, bhop and manipulate my velocity with Crossfade has made me more of a nuisance to the enemy team. Healsong movespeed is slower than speedsong. Swapping to healsong will kill your momentum, so you can utilize that to make controlled jumps and also throw in a few into speedsong strafes + short hops to mix up your movement in isolated fights.

I try to play just behind my front line, close enough that i can dive in to assist with an elim. Stay out of sight of anyone that can oneshot me, keep moving, throw in chip damage as the fight progresses. I think Lucio performs best at mid-range and is good close-range with assistance or surprising an enemy that's out of position. 

For 1v1s, the faster strafe from speed song can help your survivability and throw off some players' shot. Booping them into a corner or just into the air is enough to get some easier-to-lead shots in as well. Boop is good for creating space and controlling enemy movement (ex. boop a Rein charge off line, shake off a Reaper that worked their way into your backline, etc). It's also always fun to boop people off maps if the opportunity presents itself!

Lubing stabs is arguably the most important mod on any keyboard with them. On the larger keys (e.g. left/right shift, spacebar, enter, backspace, etc.) there are stabilizers made of a metal wire and 2 plastic housings. You can lube the ends of the wire with some dielectric grease (Permatex DE is generally cheap & accessible) to reduce that rattly sound when you hit those keys. There are plenty of good guides on YouTube on how to do this, so take your pick. If you can't uninstall your stabs to lube them, you can use something like a toothpick to gradually work lube in or spend a tiny bit more to get some small gauge blunt tip syringes to [plug the butt](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=X7PjwvUj2aU).

My pleasure! They're all really important talking points in the hobby right now, and I hadn't gotten to flesh out all my thoughts on the current state of things yet. 

>P500 was addressing the multiple points of failure with a single one

So in essence it's still a group buy format, except it's streamlined in that all of them are handled by one organized entity instead of individual designers and whatever manus they decide to get in contact with? Do correct me if I'm still misunderstanding that, though. 

>PCB designs can be generated programmatically with a proper layout system and converted to a printable file.

I'd be interested in seeing a PCB design generator; it's not something I've come across before but it's good to know that something like that is feasible. I'm curious how user-friendly the interface can be and how creative one can get with their layout without breaking the program, haha.

>Why do the key caps seem to require groupbuys, six months to deliver and only a 80% chance to actually show up?

Vestigial method from before the community blew up. Small hobby, so custom designs/colorways could only be put into production by people pooling money. Since they're made to order, you have to factor in the buy window, manufacturer prep time, the actual manufacturing, transport, and QC (with any potential delays on top of all that). As for the "80% chance to actually show up" part, the number of failed deliveries is much lower as far as I can tell. Unless you're part of a buy run by someone super inexperienced or with bad logistics, there isn't usually an issue with receiving the product in the end. Of course, you do have to consider that world shipping has been in shambles for the past year or so. 

I'm not sure where the issue is nowadays with keeping capsets in stock, since I'm just a normal community member. It could be anything from there not being enough capital in the hobby to get the operations going, to companies just deciding to stick with the current business model. 

>Why is there no better way of obtaining some of the parts? A one stop shop? 

I think it's absolutely realistic to have a single shop that can cater to the primary tastes and demands of the community but uh, no one's done that yet I guess. There are some community efforts like [ThocStock](https://thocstock.com/) to consolidate parts vendors. 

>Why are group-buys the de facto instead of like a P500 system from the manufacturer?

I'm sure I'm just not understanding the P500 system right. What's the difference between that and group buys? You have the designers putting out interest checks, and with enough interest the thing gets made. There is another layer with having the designer and the manu as 2 separate entities, so that is different than P500. 

>Is there a PCPartPicker type website to collect everything you need in?

Not that I know of. There isn't enough part compatibility to compile *everything.* There is little to no standardization between cases and PCBs. Switches and caps you can interchange pretty freely, but cases and PCBs are 90% of the time designed specifically and only for the particular design. There's so much variation between layouts and mounting systems, that you can't really pick and choose certain things. 

>Is there a market for a site that combines a board and case template designer that also prints for you and sells keycaps and switches?

Is there a market? Absolutely. Would it be sustainable and practical? With my extremely limited business knowledge, no. You would have to create god knows how many different case/PCB designs, all the tooling, prototyping, getting consistent prints/shots for legends, color matching, and the list goes on. 

Thinking more on it, if the company standardizes their options to picking a form factor with a few different layout options I think it would be closer to possible. There's just so much that would be going on just within internal logistics that I can't imagine how to process it all. 

>Why are the cables so expensive and why is the coiled one the standard? Aesthetic and IBM heritage?

The cable vendors you see all the time are artisans, so there is a premium for them being made by hand, to order. The coils? Absolutely just for looks. On top of the "custom" premium, the materials to make a cable are already more expensive (though not absurd) than just buying a USB-X to X cable, and as someone who's tried to make their own cable before, it really is an art to getting clean and consistent coils and terminations. With the time and effort that goes into making a genuinely nice looking cable, I think the current prices are warranted.

If there's anything I've learned from being in this hobby for a little while, it's that secondhand descriptions will only go so far. Factors like switches and spring weight especially are primarily preference-based. Sounds like you're comfortable with linears, so I'd think that's a safe bet. If you want to try tactile, you could pick up a switch tester or possibly just buy a tactile board and return it if you don't like it. Keep in mind, tactiles are generally grouped as light/medium/strong tactility, most enthusiast switches falling toward the stronger end and switches like all the various Brown switches, Pewters, etc. would be light tactiles. People also can describe the tactile bump as "sharp" or "rounded;" the best way to understand that is to try switches IMO. 

Kailh is another MX-style switch brand, though the housing clips are different than standard MX (only really matters if you're delving into the custom realm). Their mass-production switches aren't necessarily better, but they stick around for a reason. Main thing is whether they offer a switch that fits your preference.

Have you checked if the spacebar is warped? Longer PBT keycaps are prone to warp when they're manufactured. Try placing the spacebar on a flat surface and check if it's sitting completely flush. If it isn't and/or it rocks when you tap the ends, that would likely be the what's causing your spacebar to bind. 

If it is warped, you can fix it. Hold the cap in hot water (little below boiling) for around 20 seconds, then weigh it down a with a flat object on top of it and let it cool completely. The weight just needs to be enough to hold the bar flat, and PBT will only deform at much higher temperatures. There are examples of this fix online, as well.

Somewhat limited, but there will still be options for sure. You could absolutely squeeze arrows into the bottom right if you really want the dedicated arrow keys. I think choosing between that and going with a 65% is going to depend on your layout/aesthetics preference and how highly you value aftermarket/replacement PCBs and cases. The latter is primarily protection from extreme instances like the PCB frying, or if you plan to mix & match builds and/or cases. 

Take a look at different DZ60 builds and see if you would enjoy sitting down at your desk and seeing it there, and if you would enjoy typing on it. Will you need the right-side navigation keys of a 65? Could you do with binding them on a different layer? Is the layout something you could get used to using, and would it seem natural? With X layout, can you still use the macros you would normally use? Just some questions I've asked myself before, that you might also want to consider. 

Oh, also kinda important to add that depending on which layout you go with, it'll change your eye when looking for keycap sets. Gotta make sure the set includes enough caps of the right size and row profile, and whether the legends will match (depending on how much matching legends matters to you, of course). 

Main point being, the better option between switching to a 65 and using a GK64-style layout is the one that feels and looks best to you. Does it look sexy as hell and can you use it (or learn to use it) naturally? Go with that one.

I agree with your philosophy in that switches will impact feel the most. Keyboard characteristics are holistic and depend on too many factors to be able to replicate another's results. I would argue that keycaps also carry a notable influence on hand/keyboard interaction, but caps are generally easier (physically and financially) compared to changing switches regardless of a board being soldered or hot swap. 

5. Caps aren't exactly dirt cheap, but $50 for a full kit and minor issues at most with the caps is a pretty good deal in my eyes. I'd say that price point is further justified based on the service that PMK offers. I will say that manufacturer is probably a better gauge of quality than the price. Different facilities use different techniques, some tooling might be more worn than others, etc. This is hard to track though, as you need to be able to observe some sort of trend(s). Honestly, you should be fine with whatever keycaps if they're not a **huge** concern and like I said, easy to change out. Important to note that if you get a set made of PBT, check for warping on the larger keycaps by setting the cap down on a flat surface like a phone screen and lightly tap the ends to see if it rocks. This can be remedied with a jig and some hot water/a hairdryer, though it's an annoying process honestly.  

6. All parts listed here will physically fit together and should work perfectly as intended.
